title: Zeabur discontinues AI Hub after its August security breach
content:
In response to the security incident we confirmed on August 28, we shut down Zeabur AI Hub as a defensive measure. After further evaluation, we have decided not to bring it back and are officially discontinuing the service. Existing API keys can no longer be used to send model requests through AI Hub.
AI Hub set out to solve a specific problem: in the age of AI, people deploying AI applications shouldn't have to sign up for and manage API keys from multiple model providers across different platforms. They should be able to enable, use, and manage costs in one place through Zeabur.
After launch, we found that AI Hub did lower the barrier to building AI products. As AI applications grew rapidly, it also helped us onboard people trying these tools for the first time, as well as advanced developers who wanted to iterate quickly.
As the service kept running, however, the team re-evaluated in Q2 this year the ongoing cost of maintaining AI Hub, along with the operational and security risks that come with it.
Taking these factors into account, and in line with the product direction Zeabur wants to invest in next, we concluded that continuing to operate AI Hub is no longer the right choice, and decided to discontinue the service.
For paid balance in AI Hub that had not been used, we reconciled it against actual payment and usage records and returned it as Zeabur Credit, which you can keep using on other Zeabur services. Here is where things stand:
We understand that some of you would rather have cash than a Zeabur balance. So we are also accepting requests to convert AI Hub balances that have already been returned to your Zeabur balance into a cash refund. Just open a ticket at Zeabur Support and we will take care of the rest.
AI Hub helped many Zeabur users lower the barrier to using and managing AI models, and made it faster for more people to start deploying their own AI applications. Although AI Hub's journey ends here, the Zeabur team will keep improving the product experience and carry what we learned into Zeabur's upcoming products and services.
If you have any questions, please contact us through Zeabur Support.

report.summary: Zeabur permanently shuts down its AI Hub model API gateway after an August 28 security breach, citing security risks and unsustainable maintenance costs.
report.background: Zeabur, a deployment platform for AI applications, launched AI Hub as a unified gateway that let users enable multiple model providers, manage API keys, and track costs in one place. The product reflected a broader trend toward AI API aggregation layers—services like OpenRouter and Together that abstract away provider-by-provider signups. Such gateways lower the barrier to building AI products, but they also concentrate risk: key custody, billing reconciliation, abuse prevention, and a single point of failure. After a confirmed security incident on August 28, Zeabur shut AI Hub down defensively, then re-evaluated in Q2 the ongoing maintenance cost, operational exposure, and whether the service still fit its product roadmap. The team concluded it did not, making the shutdown permanent rather than temporary.
key_points: The August 28 security incident forced an immediate defensive shutdown of AI Hub. After review, Zeabur decided not to restore the service, and all existing API keys immediately stopped working for model requests through the hub.

AI Hub's core promise was convenience: developers could enable models, manage credentials, and track spending in one place instead of juggling accounts and API keys across multiple model providers. Zeabur says it successfully lowered the barrier for first-time and advanced builders.

Zeabur had already begun reassessing AI Hub in Q2, weighing maintenance costs, operational complexity, and security risks. The breach accelerated a decision that was already forming as the company shifted product direction.

Unused paid balances were reconciled against payment and usage records and returned as Zeabur Credit usable elsewhere on the platform. Users who prefer cash can open a support ticket to convert the balance into a refund.
report.impact: The shutdown signals that AI gateway and aggregation layers are now under real security scrutiny. Convenience abstractions that hold provider keys and route traffic become high-value targets, and a single incident can end a product line. For developers, the immediate cost is migration: re-issuing provider keys, updating environment variables, and rebuilding cost monitoring that AI Hub handled. Many will move to direct provider APIs or dedicated gateways with stronger isolation. For regular users, the change is mostly invisible except for refunds and lost one-click setup. The broader lesson is that security must be designed into AI infrastructure from day one, not treated as an operational afterthought—especially for platforms bundling billing and model access.
report.tools: If you relied on AI Hub, consider OpenRouter for multi-model access with unified billing, LiteLLM as an open-source proxy for managing provider keys and fallbacks, Portkey for gateway observability and guardrails, Cloudflare AI Gateway for caching and rate limiting, or One API/New API for self-hosted aggregation. For migration hygiene, use dotenv and secret managers to rotate keys, and add logging around model calls to replace the cost visibility AI Hub provided.
